title: Architecture and Standards Integrated Guidelines (API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, ADRs)
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and standards across API design, coding and repo conventions, infrastructure and IaC, model-serving requirements, observability practices, performance targets, and a curated list of active Architecture Decision Records (ADRs). It is intended for service owners, platform engineers, infra, and product teams who must build and operate production-grade inference services that conform to company-wide reliability, security, and cost objectives.

## Goals
- Provide a single, opinionated reference for building services that are predictable to operate and easy to audit.
- Reduce friction for model onboarding and runtime deployments by standardizing packaging, versioning, and rollout policies.
- Ensure consistent observability and SLOs across the stack so platform tooling and dashboards work out-of-the-box.
- Balance latency, cost, and accuracy through measurable performance standards and benchmarking.

## Ownership and Scope
- Document owner: eng-platform (primary contact: Maya Chen)
- Audience: service owners, infra engineers, runtime and SRE teams, product managers onboarding models
- Applicability: applies to all public-facing Redwood services and internal inference runtimes; exceptions must be approved via ADR and recorded in the ADR registry.

-----

## 1) API Standards
Purpose: Keep our developer-facing and service-to-service APIs stable, discoverable, and backwards-compatible while enabling safe iteration.

Key principles:
1. Versioning:
   - All externally visible HTTP APIs must be versioned via the URL (e.g., /v1/generate) and by a semantic API version header X-API-Version.
   - Deprecation window: minimum 90 days for minor changes; breaking changes require a migration plan and 6+ months notice for enterprise customers.
2. Contracts and Schemas:
   - Use OpenAPI 3.1 for all REST endpoints. The OpenAPI file must live in the service repo under /api/openapi.yaml and be validated in CI.
   - JSON schema must be strict: required fields marked, additionalProperties: false for request bodies unless explicitly allowed.
3. Idempotency and Retries:
   - Long-running operations must support client-generated idempotency keys (Idempotency-Key header).
   - Retry guidance: clients should implement exponential backoff and not retry on 4xx other than 429. 5xx should be retried up to 3 times with jitter.
4. Errors and Status Codes:
   - Use problem-details JSON (RFC 7807) format. Provide machine-friendly error codes (e.g., error_code: INFER_QUOTA_EXCEEDED) in the problem details.
   - Standardize 429 behavior: include Retry-After header and ratelimit headers X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.
5. Authentication and Authorization:
   - All public APIs require token-based auth (Bearer tokens). Internal service-to-service calls should use mTLS or short-lived OIDC tokens as configured by the platform.
6. Observability contract for APIs:
   - Every API handler must emit standardized metrics: request_count, request_latency_ms (histogram), request_size_bytes, response_size_bytes, error_count by error_code. Traces must include request_id and model_version tags.

Example required fields for text generation request (OpenAPI snippet required in repo):
- model: string (required)
- input: string | array (required)
- max_tokens: integer (optional, default 256)
- temperature: number (optional, 0.0-1.5)

-----

## 2) Coding Standards and Repo Structure
Purpose: Maintain readability, testability, and predictable deployment patterns across languages and services.

Language defaults and style: 
- Python services: follow PEP8 and Black formatting; use typing annotations for public functions. CI must run pytest and mypy.
- Go services: follow gofmt and go vet; codestyle enforced via golangci-lint.
- TypeScript/frontend: follow ESLint + Prettier standards; prefer strict null checks.

Repository layout (monorepo or service repo):
- /cmd or /src — service entrypoints
- /internal or /pkg — internal packages (Go) or private modules (Python)
- /api/openapi.yaml — API contract
- /infra — local terraform modules (if any) and deployment manifests, minimal duplication of global modules
- /ci — CI pipelines and scripts
- /docs — service runbooks, ownership, and known limitations

Testing and CI:
1. Unit tests required for core logic. Aim for >70% coverage on business-critical packages.
2. Integration tests: every service must have a suite that can run against mocks in CI; model integration tests must run in a gated pipeline that uses the internal eval harness for quality checks.
3. Performance/regression tests: PRs that modify runtime-critical code require perf test runs in the benchmarking cluster (see section 6).

Security coding practices:
- Do not check in secrets. Use vault-based secrets manager and CI secret injection.
- Dependabot/renovate enabled for all repos; critical security upgrades must not be delayed more than 7 days.

Code review norms:
- At least one approver from the owning team and one from infra/platform for infra changes.
- Large changes affecting runtime or cost should include perf benchmark results and an ADR when the change is architectural.

-----

## 3) Infrastructure and IaC Standards
Purpose: Provide reproducible environments, enforce least privilege, and make capacity predictable.

IaC and provisioning:
- Terraform is the canonical IaC tool. Shared modules live in the infra-modules repo. Service-specific modules are small and reference shared modules.
- State: Use remote state with locking (Terraform Cloud or S3+DynamoDB).
- CI pipelines trigger plan and require manual approval for apply in production.

Cloud accounts and networking:
- Environment separation: dev, staging, prod in different cloud accounts or projects. Cross-account access via roles only.
- VPC design: standardized subnets per availability zone, egress-only NAT for private subnets, restricted ingress via ALBs and internal gateways.

Resource naming and tagging:
- Tagging must include: service, owner, cost_center, environment, role. Tags enforced by pre-commit hooks or CI checks.

Capacity and scaling policies:
- For Dedicated GPU pools, document min/max node counts, target utilization (70-75%) and autoscaler behaviour in terraform module inputs.
- Use cluster autoscaler with scale-down delay of 10 minutes for GPU nodes to avoid thrash.

Secrets and key management:
- Use customer KMS for Private deployments when required. Platform-managed secrets are stored in Vault; access via short-lived credentials.

Deployment strategy:
- Canary rollouts are the default for critical runtime changes. Rollout steps: 1) deploy canary (1-5% traffic), 2) monitor SLOs for 30 minutes, 3) if healthy, increase to 25%, 4) full rollout. Abort thresholds defined in runbook.

-----

## 4) Model-Serving Standards
Purpose: Standardize model packaging, quantization profiles, versioning, and compatibility so the serving runtime can make reliable optimizations and fallbacks.

Model packaging and registry:
- Models must be packaged as OCI artifacts with a manifest containing metadata: model_name, model_version (semver), architecture, tokenizer_version, quantization_profile, training_commit, eval_scores.
- Registry: models stored in the internal model registry and referenced by model id (registry://team/model:version) in service configs.

Compatibility and variants:
- Each model entry must declare compatible runtime capabilities (fp16, int8, kv-cache-enabled, attention-optimizer) and resource recommendations (vram estimate for 2048 token seq).
- Recommended quantization profiles are defined per workload in /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles.

Serving configuration:
- Model config must include default max_tokens, preferred batching window (ms), and tail-latency budget.
- All serving requests must include model_version in metrics and traces for deterministic rollout and A/B.

Rollouts and fallbacks:
- Model rollout follows the same canary procedure as infra changes.
- Automatic fallback policy: if a deployed model variant exceeds error_rate_threshold (0.5% errors over 5m) or P99 latency SLO breach, traffic must be routed to a compatible fallback variant or a smaller model to preserve availability.

Quality gates and evals:
- New model versions require a quality gate run in the eval harness. At minimum: perplexity/LL, end-to-end prompt-set score, toxicity checks, and regression tests against saved prompts.

-----

## 5) Observability Standards
Purpose: Ensure consistent telemetry for troubleshooting, SLO enforcement, and cost attribution.

Metric naming and conventions:
- Metric name pattern: <service>.<component>.<metric> (e.g., infer-runtime.kv-cache.hit_rate).
- Use standard labels: environment, region, cluster, node_type, model_name, model_version, route.
- Export histograms for latency with exponential buckets covering 1ms to 60s for open APIs.

Required telemetry per service:
1. Metrics: request_count, request_latency_ms (histogram), error_count, token_emitted_count, cost_estimate_usd (derived).
2. Traces: parent <-> child spans for request lifecycle, include request_id, model_version, batch_id. Use W3C Trace Context headers.
3. Logs: structured JSON logs with keys: timestamp, level, service, request_id, user_id (if available), model_version, message, error_code. Logs must not contain raw PII or secrets.

Dashboards and alerts:
- Each service should ship a standard dashboard template (availability, latency SLOs, error budget burn, cost per 1k tokens) to the central Grafana folder.
- Alerting thresholds: SLO burn alert at 20% error budget used in 24h, critical at 50%. Latency alerts: P99 > target_latency * 1.5 for 10m.

Tracing and correlation:
- Ensure request_id is generated at edge (API gateway) and propagated across services. Span sampling for high-traffic endpoints should be probabilistic (0.1%) with dynamic tail-sampling for errors.

Retention and costs:
- Metrics: 90 days full resolution, 365 days aggregated. Logs: 30 days for full logs, 365 days for index/alerts. High-data-volume traces may be sampled to control cost.

-----

## 6) Performance Standards and Benchmarking
Purpose: Hold changes to predictable performance budgets and quantify cost/latency tradeoffs.

SLOs and targets (for inference endpoints):
- Availability: 99.95% (prod) for hosted inference APIs.
- Latency targets vary by SLA tier: for interactive text generation (<=256 tokens) P50 < 50ms, P95 < 120ms, P99 < 300ms for optimized CPU/GPU runtimes. For high-throughput batch inference, define throughput per GPU (tokens/sec) in model compatibility entry.
- Cost targets: maintain per-token cost estimates in the product catalog; changes that increase unit cost >10% require explicit approval.

Benchmarking process:
1. Microbenchmarks: per-kernel and op-level tests run in the benchmarking-and-perf-suite.
2. System benchmarks: end-to-end generation latency and throughput measured using the standard workload generator with representative prompt distributions.
3. Regression testing: all changes affecting runtime or kernels must include before/after perf artifacts and a short analysis.

Load testing and chaos:
- Load tests are run in stage using synthetic traffic profiles before major releases. For Dedicated clusters, run canary load tests using shadow traffic mode.
- Periodic chaos exercises (game-days) target autoscaling, model fallback, and cross-AZ failure modes.

Performance budgets in PRs:
- PR templates require a performance section for runtime-affecting changes: microbenchmark results, expected impact on unit cost, and suggested mitigation if regressions are observed.

-----

## 7) ADRs (Architecture Decision Records)
Purpose: Record high-impact architectural choices, alternatives considered, and the decision rationale so future engineers can understand tradeoffs.

Active ADRs (summary list):
- ADR-2024-01: Runtime kernel selection strategy — decided to use dynamic kernel selector in infer-runtime that chooses kernels based on batch size and seq length. Owner: runtime team.
- ADR-2024-09: Model artifact format — choose OCI artifacts with embedded manifest to support provenance and reproducible deployments. Owner: applied-ml.
- ADR-2025-03: Canary rollout default policy — canonicalized the 1/30/100 canary percentages and 30 minute monitoring window. Owner: eng-sre.
- ADR-2025-10: Quantization defaults — recommended int8 for non-critical workloads and fp16 for critical low-latency production. Owner: applied-ml.
- ADR-2026-01: Telemetry retention policy — move to 90/365 metrics and 30/365 logs to balance cost and incident forensics. Owner: eng-platform.

ADR process:
1. Draft an ADR in the architecture-and-standards repo under /adrs with template: context, decision, alternatives, consequences, date, and owners.
2. Get reviews from impacted teams and an approval from eng-platform for infra-affecting decisions.
3. Publish and link the ADR from the relevant service docs.

-----

## Runbooks and Escalation (summary)
- See runbooks folder in each service repo under /docs/runbook.md for exact steps. Critical playbooks: high-error-rate fallback, model-quality regression, P99 latency regression, and GPU OOM handling.
- Oncall escalation: first responder (service owner) -> SRE oncall -> eng-platform -> applied-ml for model regressions. Contact lists maintained in oncall-and-incident-response.

## Exceptions and Change Process
- Exceptions to these standards must be documented via ADR or an exception request with justification and an expiration date.
- Major changes (affecting more than one service or cost >10% increase) require a cross-team review and a documented rollout/rollback plan.
